differential: Ménière's disease
Classic triad of unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo in a young adult fits this endolymphatic hydrops disorder.
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness over months suggests a slow-growing tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
Chronic otitis media with labyrinthitis
Prolonged middle ear infection can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, and vestibular symptoms affecting one ear.
Superior semicircular canal dehiscence
Bony defect can cause unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and vestibular symptoms including dizziness.
Labyrinthine concussion
Prior head trauma causing inner ear injury could explain the unilateral auditory and vestibular symptoms.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses.

differential: Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis
Young patient with xanthomas, sensorineural hearing loss, ataxia (unsteady gait), and bilateral facial weakness suggests this lipid storage disorder with neurological manifestations.
Neurofibromatosis type 2
Bilateral facial weakness and sensorineural hearing loss could indicate bilateral vestibular schwannomas, though cutaneous lesions are typically neurofibromas not xanthomas.
Familial hypercholesterolemia with coincidental neurological disease
Multiple xanthomas in a young patient indicate severe lipid disorder, though the constellation of neurological findings would be unusual.
Erdheim-Chester disease
Rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present with xanthomatous skin lesions and central nervous system involvement causing multiple cranial neuropathies.
Sarcoidosis
Multisystem granulomatous disease can cause cutaneous papules/plaques, bilateral facial palsy (cranial nerve VII), and audiovestibular dysfunction.
eliminated: Acoustic neuroma (unilateral vestibular schwannoma)
Bilateral facial weakness and multiple systemic cutaneous lesions make isolated unilateral schwannoma unlikely.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses (vestibular schwannomas) with facial weakness and hearing loss are pathognomonic for NF2, though the skin lesions are atypical.
Schwannomatosis
Multiple schwannomas can occur at the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory canal, explaining the bilateral masses and neurological symptoms.
Erdheim-Chester disease
This rare histiocytosis can present with bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses and characteristic xanthomatous skin lesions (yellow plaques/papules).
Xanthoma disseminatum with CNS involvement
The characteristic yellow cutaneous xanthomas combined with bilateral intracranial masses affecting cranial nerves matches this rare histiocytic disorder.
Von Hippel-Lindau disease with bilateral hemangioblastomas
Can present with bilateral posterior fossa masses and systemic manifestations, though the characteristic skin lesions are less typical.
eliminated: Acoustic neuroma (sporadic unilateral)
The bilateral nature of the masses rules out sporadic unilateral vestibular schwannoma.
Multiple sclerosis
MRI shows discrete masses rather than demyelinating plaques, and skin findings are inconsistent.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Confirmed by NF2 gene mutation, bilateral vestibular schwannomas (masses at internal auditory meatus and cerebellopontine angle), and cutaneous schwannomas.
Schwannomatosis
Multiple schwannomas are present on skin and bilaterally in cranial nerves, though the confirmed NF2 mutation makes this diagnosis less likely than NF2.
LZTR1-related schwannomatosis
Can present with multiple schwannomas and rarely bilateral vestibular schwannomas, but the confirmed NF2 mutation definitively excludes this diagnosis.
Sporadic bilateral vestibular schwannomas
Bilateral acoustic neuromas with cutaneous findings could occur sporadically, but the NF2 mutation confirms genetic etiology.
Mosaic NF2
Could explain variable presentation, though the genetic testing already confirmed NF2 mutation without specifying mosaicism.
eliminated: Neurofibromatosis type 1
No café-au-lait macules, Lisch nodules, or neurofibromas; skin lesions are schwannomas not neurofibromas; NF2 gene mutation confirmed instead of NF1.
Acoustic neuroma (unilateral/sporadic)
Bilateral masses and confirmed genetic mutation indicate hereditary syndrome rather than sporadic unilateral disease.
Cutaneous xanthomas
While yellow plaques were noted, biopsy confirmed Schwann cells not lipid-laden histiocytes.

differential: Ménière's disease
Classic triad of episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and unilateral hearing loss in a young adult fits this idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops condition.
Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma)
Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness over 6 months suggests a slow-growing tumor of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
Chronic otitis media with labyrinthitis
Progressive unilateral hearing loss with vestibular symptoms could indicate chronic middle ear infection with inner ear involvement.
Labyrinthine concussion
Post-traumatic inner ear injury can cause persistent unilateral audiovestibular symptoms lasting months.
Superior semicircular canal dehiscence
Bone defect over the superior canal can produce vertigo, hearing loss, and tinnitus, though autophony is more typical.
eliminated: None
Insufficient information at this stage to definitively rule out diagnoses.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Young adult with bilateral cranial nerve involvement (CN VIII causing sensorineural hearing loss and CN VII causing bilateral facial weakness) suggests bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (sporadic)
Sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness, and unsteady gait are classic for vestibular schwannomas, though bilateral presentation is rare without NF2.
Lyme disease (neuroborreliosis)
Can cause bilateral facial palsy (cranial nerve VII) and sensorineural hearing loss with vestibular symptoms in endemic areas.
Sarcoidosis
Neurosarcoidosis can present with bilateral cranial neuropathies (particularly CN VII), sensorineural hearing loss, and vestibular dysfunction.
Guillain-Barré syndrome (Miller Fisher variant)
Can cause bilateral facial weakness and ataxia, though the six-month duration is longer than typical acute presentation.
eliminated: Acoustic neuroma (unilateral)
Bilateral facial weakness and potentially bilateral vestibular involvement make isolated unilateral pathology unlikely.
Meniere's disease
Would not explain bilateral facial muscle weakness.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Bilateral cerebellopontine angle masses in a young patient with bilateral facial weakness is pathognomonic for NF2 with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (sporadic)
Bilateral acoustic neuromas causing sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular symptoms, though sporadic bilateral cases are extremely rare without NF2.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 with bilateral schwannomas
NF1 can rarely present with multiple schwannomas, though bilateral vestibular schwannomas are much more characteristic of NF2.
Schwannomatosis
Multiple schwannomas can occur in this condition, though bilateral vestibular involvement would be atypical and should prompt consideration of NF2 instead.
Multiple meningiomas
Bilateral cerebellopontine angle meningiomas could mimic this presentation, though less likely given the patient's age and typical location for vestibular schwannomas.
eliminated: Acoustic neuroma (unilateral sporadic)
Imaging reveals bilateral masses, ruling out a solitary unilateral lesion.
Meniere's disease
MRI findings of structural masses exclude this inner ear disorder.
Vestibular neuritis
The presence of bilateral structural masses on imaging excludes inflammatory vestibular pathology.

differential: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Genetic testing confirmed NF2 gene mutation with bilateral vestibular schwannomas and cutaneous schwannomas, pathognomonic for this condition.
Schwannomatosis
Multiple schwannomas are present, but the confirmed NF2 mutation and bilateral vestibular schwannomas make NF2 more likely than isolated schwannomatosis.
LZTR1-related schwannomatosis
This can present with multiple schwannomas and rarely vestibular involvement, but confirmed NF2 mutation makes this diagnosis less likely.
Mosaic neurofibromatosis type 2
Could present with milder or asymmetric features, but the bilateral vestibular schwannomas and germline NF2 mutation confirm classic NF2.
SMARCB1-related schwannomatosis
Multiple schwannomas can occur, but the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas and confirmed NF2 mutation excludes this diagnosis.
eliminated: Neurofibromatosis type 1
No café-au-lait macules or neurofibromas; NF2 gene mutation confirmed rather than NF1.
Acoustic neuroma (sporadic)
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas with NF2 mutation indicate hereditary syndrome rather than sporadic tumor.
Vestibular migraine
MRI shows structural lesions (schwannomas) causing symptoms, not functional disorder.
Meniere's disease
Bilateral masses on MRI and NF2 mutation explain symptoms, not endolymphatic hydrops.

counterfactuals.alteration_description: The absence of skin findings argues against neurofibromatosis, which typically presents with multiple cutaneous neurofibromas or other skin manifestations.
